You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image render the depicted forms as a drawing rather than retaining substantial photographic detail beneath drawn contours?
node.criteria: Pass if, compared with the source, the depicted forms are visibly rendered as drawn forms, with drawing-like contours or linework and without substantial photographic surface detail remaining. Fail if the image retains substantial photographic representation even where outlines or linework are added. Unknown only if the relevant representation cannot be observed.
node.source_quote: Turn the image into a drawing
node.endpoint: The depicted forms are rendered as a drawing rather than retaining substantial photographic representation.
node.necessity: The instruction requests turning the image into a drawing; outlines alone do not establish that transformation when the depicted forms still retain substantial photographic detail.

node_traces.evidence: Compared with the source photograph, the edited image renders the giraffes and surroundings with soft, grainy chalk-like shading and drawn contours; photographic surface detail in the animals, foliage, and ground is substantially reduced.

d2: The node’s criterion is already specific and the trace gives concrete visual evidence of chalk-like smudging and sketchy marks across multiple surfaces. The mismatch is not evidence that this check should fail: the image clearly shows substantial progress toward the requested chalk rendering, while the reference label `partial` concerns completion of the whole instruction, not atomic ground truth for this one requirement. Keep the required chalk-rendering check and avoid weakening it or forcing a negative result. Improve the decision node’s scope or routing so this material-appearance check contributes evidence of progress without alone implying that every requested change is complete; reserve the aggregate `yes`/`partial` judgment for evaluating all requested changes together. Treat the high-confidence pass as valid visual evidence, not as a transport or dependency failure.
